blocks.body:
Dirichlet proved that $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$. Every quantitative use of $L$-functions needs more: how small can $L(1,\chi)$ be, and how close to $s=1$ can a zero of $L(s,\chi)$ lie? For complex characters, and for zeros off the real axis, the classical zero-free region gives a satisfactory answer. One possibility has resisted all attempts at exclusion: a real character $\chi$ modulo $q$ whose $L$-function has a real zero $\beta$ extremely close to $1$. Such a hypothetical zero is called a Siegel zero (also an exceptional or Landau–Siegel zero).

Nobody expects Siegel zeros to exist; the generalized Riemann hypothesis would rule them out completely. But the question of excluding them unconditionally has for decades been one of the central open problems of analytic number theory, and the best unconditional result, Siegel's theorem of 1935, comes with a constant that no one knows how to compute.

blocks.title: Where the exceptional zero comes from
blocks.body:
The zero-free region for Dirichlet $L$-functions (see [[zero-free-region]]) has a gap in it. The standard statement, due to Landau and Page, reads as follows; we do not prove it here.

There is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for every $q$, the product $\prod_{\chi \bmod q}L(s,\chi)$ has at most one zero $s = \sigma + it$ in the region
$$\sigma > 1 - \frac{c}{\log\bigl(q(|t|+2)\bigr)}.$$
If this zero exists, it is real and simple, and it is a zero of $L(s,\chi_1)$ for a real non-principal character $\chi_1$.

The proof of the zero-free region uses the inequality $3 + 4\cos\theta + \cos2\theta \ge 0$ applied to $L(s,\chi_0)^3L(s+it,\chi)^4L(s+2it,\chi^2)$. When $\chi$ is real and $t$ is close to $0$, the character $\chi^2$ is principal and $L(s+2it,\chi^2)$ has a pole near $s=1$ instead of being harmless, and the argument breaks down. That single gap is the exceptional zero.

blocks.title: Siegel zero
blocks.body:
Let $\chi$ be a real primitive character modulo $q$ and $\beta$ a real zero of $L(s,\chi)$. Informally, $\beta$ is a Siegel zero if $1-\beta$ is small compared with $1/\log q$. Precisely, Siegel zeros exist if there is a sequence of real primitive characters $\chi_j$ modulo $q_j$ with real zeros $\beta_j$ such that
$$(1-\beta_j)\log q_j \to 0.$$
The Landau–Siegel problem asks to prove that there are none, that is, that $\beta \le 1 - c/\log q$ for some absolute $c>0$ and all such zeros.

blocks.title: Real zeros near 1 make L(1, χ) small
blocks.body:
A zero close to $1$ and a small value at $1$ are two forms of the same phenomenon.

Lemma. Let $\chi$ be non-principal modulo $q \ge 8$. For $1 - \frac{1}{\log q} \le \sigma \le 1$ we have $|L'(\sigma,\chi)| \le C\log^2 q$ with an absolute constant $C$.

Proof. $L'(\sigma,\chi) = -\sum_n \chi(n)(\log n)n^{-\sigma}$. For $n \le q$ we have $n^{1-\sigma} \le q^{1/\log q} = e$, so the terms with $n \le q$ contribute at most $e\sum_{n\le q}\frac{\log n}{n} \le e\log q\,(1+\log q)$. For $n>q$ the function $t \mapsto (\log t)t^{-\sigma}$ is decreasing (since $q \ge 8 > e^{1/\sigma}$), so the partial-summation bound from [[l-functions]] gives at most $2\varphi(q)(\log q)q^{-\sigma} \le 2e\log q$. Adding up gives the claim.

Consequence. If $L(\beta,\chi)=0$ with $1-\frac{1}{\log q} \le \beta < 1$, the mean value theorem gives a $\sigma \in (\beta,1)$ with
$$L(1,\chi) = L(1,\chi) - L(\beta,\chi) = (1-\beta)L'(\sigma,\chi),\quad\text{so}\quad L(1,\chi) \le C(1-\beta)\log^2 q.$$
Read backwards: any lower bound for $L(1,\chi)$ gives a zero-free interval to the left of $1$,
$$1-\beta \ \ge\ \frac{L(1,\chi)}{C\log^2 q}.$$
For $D<-4$ the [[class-number-formula]] gives $L(1,\chi_D) = \pi h(D)/\sqrt{|D|} \ge \pi/\sqrt{|D|}$, so a real zero satisfies $1 - \beta \ge \pi/(C\sqrt{|D|}\log^2|D|)$. This is effective, but far weaker than the $c/\log q$ one would like. (For positive discriminants the formula $L(1,\chi_D) = 2h(D)\log\varepsilon_D/\sqrt D$ gives a bound of the same quality.)

blocks.title: Siegel's theorem (1935)
blocks.body:
For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a constant $c(\varepsilon)>0$ such that for every real primitive character $\chi$ modulo $q$,
$$L(1,\chi) > c(\varepsilon)\,q^{-\varepsilon}.$$
Consequently every real zero $\beta$ of $L(s,\chi)$ satisfies
$$1 - \beta \;\gg_\varepsilon\; q^{-\varepsilon},$$
and for $D<0$ the class number satisfies $h(D) \gg_\varepsilon |D|^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. For $\varepsilon < \frac12$ no established proof allows $c(\varepsilon)$ to be computed.

blocks.title: Why the constant cannot be computed
blocks.body:
The consequences follow from the main inequality: by the lemma, $1-\beta \ge c(\varepsilon)q^{-\varepsilon}/(C\log^2q)$, which is $\gg_\varepsilon q^{-2\varepsilon}$, and $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary; the class number bound is the class number formula. The interesting part is the main inequality. We describe the structure of the proof without the estimates (a short complete version is Goldfeld's, presented in Davenport, Chapter 21).

Take two distinct real primitive characters $\chi_1$, $\chi_2$ and form
$$F(s) = \zeta(s)L(s,\chi_1)L(s,\chi_2)L(s,\chi_1\chi_2).$$
This is the Dedekind zeta function of a biquadratic field. Its Dirichlet coefficients are non-negative, its first coefficient is $1$, and its residue at $s=1$ is $\lambda = L(1,\chi_1)L(1,\chi_2)L(1,\chi_1\chi_2)$. An inequality for Dirichlet series with these properties shows: if $F(\beta) \le 0$ for some $\beta$ close to $1$, then $\lambda$ cannot be much smaller than $(1-\beta)$ times a negative power $(q_1q_2)^{-O(1-\beta)}$.

Now split into two cases, depending on $\varepsilon$.

1. Some real primitive character $\chi_1$ has a real zero $\beta_1 \in (1-\varepsilon, 1)$. Fix one. For every other $\chi_2$ we have $F(\beta_1) = 0$, and the inequality gives a lower bound for $L(1,\chi_2)$ of the shape $c(\chi_1)\,q_2^{-O(\varepsilon)}$, where $c(\chi_1)$ depends on $q_1$ and $\beta_1$.
2. No real character has a zero in $(1-\varepsilon,1)$. Then $L(\beta,\chi) > 0$ on that interval for every real non-principal $\chi$ (it is positive at $\beta = 1$, as in the first example below, and has no zero in the interval), while $\zeta(\beta) < 0$ for $0<\beta<1$. So $F(\beta) < 0$ for every $\beta \in (1-\varepsilon,1)$, and the inequality again bounds $L(1,\chi_2)$ from below.

In both cases $L(1,\chi) \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$. But in case 1 the constant depends on the character $\chi_1$, and we do not know whether case 1 happens at all, let alone which $\chi_1$ to take. That is the source of the ineffectivity: the proof is a proof by cases where one case may be empty and the other has an unknown parameter.

A partial remedy is due to Tatuzawa (1951): the inequality holds with an explicitly computable constant for all real primitive characters with at most one exception. Landau had earlier shown a related repulsion: two distinct real primitive characters cannot both have real zeros very close to $1$; there is an absolute $c$ with $\min(\beta_1,\beta_2) \le 1 - c/\log(q_1q_2)$.

blocks.title: What a Siegel zero would do
blocks.body:
1. Primes in progressions. In the explicit formula for primes in progressions modulo $q$, an exceptional zero $\beta_1$ of $L(s,\chi_1)$ contributes a secondary term, roughly
$$\psi(x;q,a) \approx \frac{x}{\varphi(q)}\bigl(1 - \chi_1(a)\,x^{\beta_1-1}\bigr).$$
If $\beta_1$ is very close to $1$, then $x^{\beta_1-1}$ stays close to $1$ for a long range of $x$: classes with $\chi_1(a) = 1$ are almost empty of primes and classes with $\chi_1(a) = -1$ receive almost twice their share. See [[siegel-walfisz]].

2. Class numbers. $h(D) = \sqrt{|D|}\,L(1,\chi_D)/\pi$ would be unusually small.

3. Repulsion of other zeros (the Deuring–Heilbronn phenomenon). An exceptional zero pushes the other zeros of all $L$-functions of nearby moduli away from $s=1$. This is so strong that a Siegel zero has some surprisingly good consequences: Heath-Brown (1983) proved that if Siegel zeros exist, then there are infinitely many twin primes.

That last point explains part of the difficulty: a Siegel zero leads to no visible contradiction, and in other respects it makes primes very regular.

blocks.title: Status
blocks.body:
Unconditionally, Siegel's theorem is the established general result, together with effective but much weaker bounds such as the one derived above. Under [[grh]] there are no Siegel zeros at all, since every non-trivial zero then has real part $\frac12$. Excluding them unconditionally, a statement much weaker than GRH, has been a central open problem since the 1930s.

On 6 October 2026, OpenAI released 372 result families on GitHub, among them a short paper claiming to exclude Siegel zeros. Three manuscripts were withdrawn the next day over a sign error. This is an AI-generated claim. Until it has been independently checked, the exclusion of Siegel zeros should be treated as claimed, not established; [[no-siegel]] tracks the claim.

blocks.title: Real zeros in the half-plane of convergence lie in (0, 1)
blocks.body: Let $\chi$ be a real non-principal character. Show that $L(\sigma,\chi) > 0$ for all real $\sigma \ge 1$. Deduce that any real zero with $\sigma > 0$ (where the series converges) lies in $(0,1)$.
blocks.solution:
For $\sigma>1$, each Euler factor $(1-\chi(p)p^{-\sigma})^{-1}$ is a positive real number, because $\chi(p) \in \{-1,0,1\}$ and $p^{-\sigma}<1$. Equivalently, $L(\sigma,\chi) = e^{\ell(\sigma,\chi)}$ where $\ell(\sigma,\chi) = \sum_p\sum_k \chi(p)^k/(kp^{k\sigma})$ is real. So $L(\sigma,\chi) > 0$ for $\sigma>1$.

At $\sigma = 1$: $L(\sigma,\chi)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, so $L(1,\chi) = \lim_{\sigma\to1^+}L(\sigma,\chi) \ge 0$, and Dirichlet's theorem says $L(1,\chi) \ne 0$. Hence $L(1,\chi)>0$. So a real zero with $\sigma>0$ must lie in $(0,1)$, and the question is whether it can approach $1$ from the left. (The analytic continuation of $L(s,\chi)$ does have real zeros with $\sigma \le 0$, the trivial zeros at $0$ or the negative integers, but those play no role here.)

blocks.title: How small is L(1, χ_D) in practice?
blocks.body: Find the smallest values of $L(1,\chi_D)$ over fundamental discriminants $-5000 < D < -4$, and look at $L(\sigma,\chi_{-163})$ for real $\sigma<1$.

blocks.title: The size of the effect
blocks.body: Suppose, hypothetically, that a real character $\chi_1$ modulo $q$ had a zero at $\beta_1 = 1 - \frac{1}{100\log q}$, and ignore all other zeros. Using the approximate formula above, what share of its expected number of primes would a class $a$ with $\chi_1(a) = 1$ receive at $x = q^{10}$?
blocks.solution: We have $x^{\beta_1 - 1} = \exp\bigl(-\frac{\log x}{100\log q}\bigr) = \exp(-\frac{10}{100}) = e^{-0.1} \approx 0.905$. So the class would receive about $1 - 0.905 \approx 0.095$ of its share $x/\varphi(q)$, and a class with $\chi_1(a) = -1$ about $1.905$ of its share. Only when $\log x$ is many times $100\log q$ does the distortion fade, so a zero of this strength would distort the primes modulo $q$ up to about $x = q^{100}$ and beyond, that is, for moduli as large as a fixed power of $x$. For moduli $q \le (\log x)^A$ Siegel's bound $1-\beta \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ shows the effect is negligible, but only with an ineffective constant: this is the content of [[siegel-walfisz]].

blocks.body:
- Siegel's bound is ineffective: it proves $h(D) \to \infty$ at a rate $|D|^{1/2-\varepsilon}$, but it cannot tell you from which $|D|$ on, say, $h(D) > 10$. Explicit class number tables come from other methods.
- A Siegel zero is not merely a zero off the critical line. Any real zero in $(\frac12,1)$ would contradict GRH, but a Siegel zero must be closer to $1$ than $c/\log q$. Excluding Siegel zeros is much weaker than GRH.
- In $1-\beta \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ the implied constant depends on $\varepsilon$ and is not computable; it is not an absolute constant.

Siegel's theorem feeds directly into the [[siegel-walfisz]] theorem on primes in progressions to moduli up to a power of $\log x$, and through it into [[bombieri-vinogradov]] and the [[ternary-goldbach]] problem; the ineffective constant propagates into all of them. The link with class numbers is the [[class-number-formula]]. The hoped-for result, that Siegel zeros do not exist, is the subject of [[no-siegel]]; it would follow from [[grh]]. Heath-Brown's theorem connects the problem to [[twin-primes]].

1. Show that if $L(1,\chi) \ge c/\log q$ for all real primitive $\chi$ with an absolute $c>0$, then every real zero satisfies $1-\beta \ge c'/\log^3 q$.
2. Let $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ be prime and $\chi(n) = \bigl(\frac{n}{p}\bigr)$. Using the Euler product heuristically, explain why a very small value of $L(1,\chi)$ suggests that $\chi(\ell) = -1$ for most small primes $\ell$.
3. In the two-case proof of Siegel's theorem, identify exactly which quantity the final constant depends on and why it cannot be bounded explicitly.
4. Check that $h(-163) = 1$ by listing the reduced forms of discriminant $-163$, and compare $L(1,\chi_{-163})$ with the lower bound $\pi/\sqrt{|D|}$.

sources.ref: D. R. Heath-Brown, Prime twins and Siegel zeros, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (1983)
